newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Panamco sees further growth this year.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Panamco sees further growth this year.

text.p: Just about the only worry analysts have about Coca-Cola bottling giant Panamerican Beverages Inc these days is that its aggressive chairman smokes too much.

Panamco, as the company is known, has grown by leaps and bounds in the past decade to become the world's second largest soft-drink bottler and the biggest in Latin America -- reaching annual sales last year of $2 billion.

Panamco Chairman Francisco Sanchez-Loaeza, in an interview with Reuters on Thursday, sounded almost sheepish in explaining the hungry pace of expansion at Panamco, which in May bought out the local Coca-Cola bottler in Venezuela and now controls almost 90 percent of that soft drink market.
"We don't want to eat up the world. We are part of a process of consolidation in the industry that will happen with or without Panamco," Sanchez-Loaeza said.

But the company has no intention of slowing down and is turning its sights to smaller Coke bottlers in Mexico, Brazil and Central America, where it has a bottling operation in Costa Rica, but is casting its net in neighboring countries.
Panamco is currently in talks with three or four bottlers in Latin America -- Sanchez-Loaeza would not say where -- and expects to wrap up at least one or two of the deals this year.
The company has a low debt-to-capital ratio, about 20 percent, and has an investment grade rating -- meaning it can tap debt markets easily to fund new acquisitions.

Panamco is still doing due diligence on the recent deal in Venezuela, where it paid about $100 million in cash and exchanged about 30.6 million of its shares to the Coca-Cola Co and the Cisneros Group of Companies.
Despite some fears of dilution, Sanchez-Loaeza said the overall deal could be either slightly dilutive or accretive, given the company's projections for growth in Venezuela.
"It was not cheap, but the price was fair," he said of the Coca Cola y Hit de Venezuela purchase.
Panamco will spend roughly the same amount in Venezuela this year as they do in other major markets -- between $60 and $100 million, he said.
Pepsi Co, which used Cisneros as its local bottler in Venezuela until they defected to Coke earlier this year, has reentered the market through brewing and foods group Polar.
"Brand preference is still fairly strong. It's one thing to paint the trucks red instead of blue, but it's another to convince 22 million people to change," he said.
In Mexico, Panamco sales this year should surpass record levels set in 1994, evidence the economy here is slowly recovering from its recent crisis, Sanchez-Loaeza said.
In addition to an economic recovery in Latin America, the company will also boost volumes by keeping its focus on marketing tools, such as coolers and vending machines.
"Wherever people spend five minutes of their time -- in a beauty salon, in a bank, at a bus stop -- we can sell Coke," he said.
Panamco is keen to list its shares on the local bourses of Mexico and Brazil in order to raise the profile of the company, he said.
Investors have rewarded Panamco for its moves. The stock, which had a IPO price of $27 per share last year, split and is back up to about $31.

"These guys are following in the footsteps of Coke Enterprises (the Atlanta-based Coca-Cola anchor bottler). I can't think of any major problems they have," Francisco Rivero, a food and beverage analyst at Smith Barney, told Reuters.
"Well, maybe Francisco smokes too much," he said jokingly, referring to Sanchez-Loaeza.
As far as the cigarrettes go, Sanchez-Loaeza said he is trying to cut down. He smoked about five during the two-hour interview.

But while Pepsi would likely win back some lost market share, he estimated Panamco would end up with about 85 percent of the soft drink market in Venezuela and produce about 200 million cases of 24 8-oz. servings this year.
"Venezuela is recovering nicely and there should be a bigger pie for everyone," he said.
Panamco will also start distributing Cisneros Group's Regional brand beer in Venezuela by year end, adding about $10-$15 million a year in operating profits, he said.
